prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, which opened a new regime of frequency and time measurement at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: Having read all eight openings, I move B002 ahead of my own opening first choice, B043. B002 is the only shortlisted candidate that seven of eight members ranked, and it is first for two of us and in the top three for three. That breadth matters, but I am not counting votes. The scientific case holds up on its own: the magic-wavelength lattice removes the trapping-light shift, so many atoms can be interrogated at once without perturbing the clock transition. Independent groups (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, NIST, PTB, SYRTE) now agree at the 10^-18 level, and that agreement is the standard of independent confirmation I look for. It has opened new observations: millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, relativistic geodesy, searches for varying constants and dark matter, and a credible path to redefining the second. The credit is also unusually clean, with Katori for the concept and first Sr lattice clocks and Ye for taking accuracy and stability to the limit. That is a two-person prize that does not require us to arbitrate a collaboration or a theory-versus-experiment split. The 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize are adjacent but recognise different achievements.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that a clock may read as technology and incremental refinement of a lineage the Academy has already honoured (Ramsey, Hall and Hansch, Wineland and Haroche), rather than as a discovery about nature. Ye already shared the 2005 prize, and the redefinition of the second has not happened. I also cannot judge the atomic-physics priority questions, such as parallel magic-wavelength ideas or Sr and Yb community contributions, from my own expertise, so I rely on Eva Lindroth and Stefan Kroll for that. If the committee wants a first-of-its-kind discovery about nature, B043 is the stronger statement, and B053 is the more consequential one if a rule-compliant credit set can be found.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B002 first as a measurement instrument that changed what can be measured, and worries about overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes and about waiting for the redefinition of the second.
responses.response: I agree with the instrument-first reading, since I judge precision work by new technique plus control of systematics and the clocks pass both tests. I do not think we should wait for the redefinition: it is a metrological and political decision, and the physics was settled by the cross-lab agreement years ago. I do differ on one point. 'Changed what can be measured' is necessary but not sufficient, so the citation should name the physical regime opened, not only the instrument. I would also take your atom interferometry ranking (B012) seriously as a later candidate, but it is not on the shortlist, so I do not argue it here.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B002 first because magic-wavelength trapping turned atomic spectroscopy into a precision test of time and redshift, but says the committee must show the new content is distinct from Wineland and Hall, and has not independently checked that Katori was first with the magic-wavelength proposal.
responses.response: I defer to you on the priority question, and it is the one open point I would want settled before a final ballot. If parallel proposals of the magic wavelength exist, the committee should check them against the original papers instead of assuming. On distinctness I think the answer is straightforward: 2005 was about the comb as a frequency ruler and 2012 about manipulating single quantum systems, while the lattice clock is a many-atom scheme that beats the quantum projection noise limit of single-ion clocks. I would put that contrast into the motivation.

responses.point: Olsson ranks IceCube fifth because source identification is still limited and there is some risk of premature recognition, and she notes that DUMAND, Baikal and AMANDA pioneers are not credited.
responses.response: This is a fair challenge to my own opening first choice and it is part of why I now put B043 as an alternative instead of my lead. My answer is that the discovery is the diffuse astrophysical flux of 2013, already seen in several channels and corroborated independently, not the unresolved question of where most neutrinos come from. The 2002 prize for cosmic neutrinos shows the Academy has accepted a window-opening result before its sources were mapped. But your attribution point is real: naming Halzen and Spiering leaves out DUMAND and Baikal pioneers, and that is a cost B002 does not carry.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the Higgs observation (B053) first as the overdue discovery-first case, with the founding spokespersons of ATLAS and CMS as a defensible three-person set, and ranks IceCube second.
responses.response: I share your view that the discovery is unquestionable and that the 2013 prize left the experimental half open, and I placed B053 second on my own opening ballot. Where I disagree is on attribution. The three names are founders and spokespersons of two collaborations of thousands, and Eva Olsson is right that this is not the same as identifying who made the decisive measurement. Statute allows three people, so we would credit the instrument-building leadership, not the 2012 analysis. I can support that only if the committee is willing to state openly that the citation rewards leadership of the detectors, and I am not sure it is. That is why I keep B053 as an alternative and not as my lead.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards optical lattice clocks as a distinct discovery or as the continuation of the Ramsey, Hall and Wineland clock lineage.
Priority of the magic-wavelength proposal and the contributions of the wider Sr and Yb lattice-clock community, which I cannot check myself.
Whether the IceCube diffuse-flux result alone is a sufficient prize motivation if source identification is judged premature, and how to credit the DUMAND, Baikal and AMANDA pioneers.
Whether a rule-compliant, defensible three-person credit for the Higgs observation exists.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for B002 from my profile. As Chair, I note that I am a member of PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur and work in astroparticle physics, so I am close to the field of B043 and to antimatter work such as B063, and I trained at CERN, which is near B053. I have no stated collaboration with any named candidate on the shortlist, but the committee should weigh that proximity when it considers my views on those entries.
